All topics · Statistics · Lesson 9 · C&B Chapter 1 summary

Chapter 1 summary: independence again, densities, and the whole chapter on one page

Two days. Day 1 (about 30 minutes): the reading and Parts 1–3. Day 2 (about 15 minutes): Parts 4–5. Three wins: say what independence means and test it by computing both sides; say what a pdf's value is; state Chapter 1's main results from memory and what each is for.

Why this lesson

Chapter 1 is the ground everything else stands on. Every later chapter computes expectations, transformations and sampling distributions, and almost every one assumes the observations are independent and identically distributed. Before moving on, this lesson does three things: it fixes the two ideas that haven't landed yet (what independence means, and what a density's value means), it teaches the one Chapter 1 definition we skipped (identically distributed), and it puts the whole chapter on one page so you can recall it without the book.

Read first (about 8 minutes)

Reading

Casella & Berger, two short slices:

  1. §1.3, pp. 25–26: from "In some cases it may happen that the occurrence of a particular event, B, has no effect on the probability of another event, A" through the proof of Theorem 1.3.9. Stop at "Independence of more than two events". That's the motivation for independence, Definition 1.3.7, Example 1.3.8 (de Méré's dice) and Theorem 1.3.9 with its proof of part (a).
  2. §1.5, pp. 33–34: Definition 1.5.8, Example 1.5.9 and the statement of Theorem 1.5.10. Skip the proof of 1.5.10's hard direction (the book says it needs more machinery).

Notation traps. The scan of this book often prints \(P(A)\) as "peA)" and \(P(B)\) as "PCB)"; in your copy they're ordinary \(P(A)\), \(P(B)\). In Theorem 1.3.9, \(B^c\) is the complement of \(B\). In Definition 1.5.8, \(\mathcal{B}\) is the collection of sets of real numbers we're allowed to ask about (intervals, their countable unions and so on); read "every set \(A \in \mathcal{B}\)" as "every set of numbers you'd ever ask about".

Answer the boxes below as you read, a sentence or two each.

Casella & Berger start independence from \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\), then take \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) as the definition. In your own words: what does the first form say, and why do they prefer the second as the definition?

Reading note; reply to it. First form: learning that B happened leaves the probability of A unchanged. They prefer the product form because it treats A and B symmetrically, generalizes to more than two events, and (beyond the reading) needs no P(B) > 0.

In Example 1.5.9, \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed, but the book says "for no sample points do we have \(X(s) = Y(s)\)". How can both be true?

Reading note; reply to it. Identically distributed is about probabilities: P(X ∈ A) = P(Y ∈ A) for every set A (same cdf). It says nothing about the two functions agreeing outcome by outcome. With three tosses, heads = tails would need 1.5 of each, so X(s) ≠ Y(s) always.

Which earlier theorem does the book's proof of Theorem 1.3.9(a) use in its first step, and what does that step give?

Reading note; reply to it. Theorem 1.2.9(a): P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B). Then independence replaces P(A ∩ B) with P(A)P(B), and factoring gives P(A)(1 − P(B)) = P(A)P(Bᶜ).

One thing that surprised or confused you.

Part 1 · Independence means the probability doesn't change (re-teach, about 10 minutes)

From the reading, with an example beyond it. Lesson 8 separated disjoint from independent. This part is about the definition itself. A common wrong reading is "independent means both can happen; dependent means one forces the other". That's a statement about which outcomes go together. Independence is a statement about probabilities, and the two come apart. Here is the example where they come apart.

Recap: conditional probability (lesson 7). \(P(B \mid A) = P(A \cap B)/P(A)\) when \(P(A) > 0\): the probability of \(B\) once you know \(A\) happened, computed by shrinking the sample space to \(A\).

The setup. Roll two fair dice. \(A\) = the first die shows 6. \(B\) = the sum is 7. Once you know \(A\), the sum is 7 exactly when the second die shows 1. So knowing \(A\) tells you which second roll you need. Does that make \(A\) and \(B\) dependent?

Compute the probability of \(B\) with no information. Six of the 36 equally likely rolls sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So \(P(B) = 6/36 = 1/6\).

Compute it again after learning \(A\). Shrink to the 6 rolls with first die 6; one of them, (6,1), sums to 7. So \(P(B \mid A) = 1/6\). The same number. Learning \(A\) changed which outcome you need, but not the chance of getting it. So \(A\) and \(B\) are independent. (Product check: \(P(A \cap B) = 1/36 = \frac16 \cdot \frac16\).)

Now the sum is 12. With no information, \(P(\text{sum } 12) = 1/36\): only (6,6). After learning \(A\), the sum is 12 exactly when the second die shows 6, so \(P(\text{sum } 12 \mid A) = 1/6\). The chance went from 1/36 to 1/6. Dependent.

Why the difference? In both cases, knowing \(A\) pins down which second roll is needed, and in both cases that roll has probability 1/6. What differs is the before: every first-die value has exactly one partner that makes 7, so "sum is 7" was already 1/6; only one first-die value can make 12, so "sum is 12" was much rarer. Dependence is a change in probability, and you can only see it by computing both numbers.

Say it this way: "A and B are independent when learning that A happened doesn't change the probability of B: \(P(B \mid A) = P(B)\), or equivalently \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\)." Not this: "A and B are independent when they can happen together", or "dependent means one forces the other". The test is always arithmetic: compute both sides.

Two fair dice are rolled. \(A\) = the first die shows an even number. \(B\) = the sum is 8. What is \(P(B \mid A)\)? (A fraction, a decimal to three places, or an expression such as 3/18; * for ×, / for division.)

Of the 18 rolls with an even first die, three sum to 8: (2,6), (4,4), (6,2). So \(P(B \mid A) = 3/18 = 1/6\). With no information, \(P(B) = 5/36\) (five rolls sum to 8), so learning \(A\) raised the chance from \(5/36 \approx 0.139\) to \(1/6 \approx 0.167\): these events are dependent, even though neither forces the other.

A fair 12-sided die has faces 1 to 12. \(E\) = the roll is even; \(M\) = the roll is a multiple of 3. Are \(E\) and \(M\) independent?

\(P(E) = 6/12\), \(P(M) = 4/12\) (3, 6, 9, 12), and \(E \cap M = \{6, 12\}\), so \(P(E \cap M) = 2/12 = \frac12 \cdot \frac13\). Independent. Sharing outcomes doesn't make events dependent (independent events with positive probability must share some), and knowing \(E\) does change which faces are possible: what matters is whether the probability of \(M\) changes. Here it stays 1/3.

Two fair dice. Given that the first die shows 3, the sum is 7 exactly when the second die shows 4. Explain, using probabilities, why "the first die shows 3" and "the sum is 7" are still independent.

Got it: computes (or states) P(sum 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 and P(sum 7 | first die 3) = 1/6 (only (3,4)), and concludes independent because the probability doesn't change (or the product check 1/36 = 1/6 · 1/6). Not yet: argues from "it can happen" / "it doesn't force" without the two probabilities, or calls them dependent because the first die decides which second roll is needed.

Proof: complements of independent events

From the reading. Theorem 1.3.9 says that if \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, so are \(A\) and \(B^c\); the book proves this part (a) with Theorem 1.2.9(a), \(P(A \cap B^c) = P(A) - P(A \cap B)\).

Recap: Theorem 1.2.9(a) (lesson 6). For any events, \(P(B \cap A^c) = P(B) - P(A \cap B)\): split \(B\) into the disjoint pieces \(B \cap A\) and \(B \cap A^c\) and use Axiom 3.

Casella & Berger, Exercise 1.40 (part b). Prove: if \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, then \(A^c\) and \(B\) are independent. Name each fact you use.

Full marks: P(Aᶜ ∩ B) = P(B) − P(A ∩ B) (Theorem 1.2.9a, or the disjoint split of B with Axiom 3) = P(B) − P(A)P(B) (independence) = P(B)(1 − P(A)) = P(B)P(Aᶜ) (complement rule). Got it: all steps present, a citation missing. Not yet: assumes what is to be proved (uses P(Aᶜ ∩ B) = P(Aᶜ)P(B) along the way), or argues in words that "complements carry no information" without the algebra.

\(P(A^c \cap B) = P(B) - P(A \cap B) = P(B) - P(A)P(B) = P(B)\,(1 - P(A)) = P(A^c)\,P(B)\). The first step is Theorem 1.2.9(a), the second is independence of \(A\) and \(B\), the last is the complement rule.

Part 2 · A pdf's value is a density, not a probability (re-teach, about 6 minutes)

From lesson 8's reading (§1.6), with an example beyond it. A pdf's value is often mistaken for \(P(X = x)\). That's true of a pmf only. The key fact is from §1.6: for a continuous random variable, \(P(X = x) = 0\) at every \(x\). So the pdf's value can't be that probability; if it were, the pdf would be 0 everywhere.

A density bigger than 1. Let \(X\) be uniform on \([0, \tfrac12]\): its pdf is \(f(x) = 2\) there and 0 elsewhere (the area, \(2 \times \tfrac12\), is 1). So \(f(0.3) = 2\). That can't be a probability.

What it is. Take a short interval starting at 0.3: \(P(0.3 < X \le 0.3 + h) = 2h\) for small \(h\). The probability of a short interval is about density × length. So \(f(x)\) is probability per unit length near \(x\), the way kilograms per litre is mass per unit volume.

And a single point. Shrink the interval to nothing: \(h \to 0\) gives \(P(X = 0.3) = 0\), while \(f(0.3)\) stays 2. Point probability and density are different quantities; only the pmf, for a discrete \(X\), is point probability.

Say it this way: "A pdf's value is a density: probability per unit length. Probabilities come from areas under it." Not this: "\(f(x)\) is the probability that \(X = x\)."

A continuous random variable \(X\) has pdf \(f\) with \(f(0.4) = 1.5\), and \(f\) is continuous near 0.4. Which statement is true?

For a short interval, probability ≈ density × length = \(1.5 \times 0.01 = 0.015\). A single point has probability 0 for a continuous \(X\), and a density may exceed 1 as long as the total area is 1: uniform on \([0, \tfrac23]\) has \(f = 1.5\) everywhere there. Why the stem says "continuous near 0.4": changing a pdf at one point changes no probability, so a single value means something only where \(f\) is continuous, and continuity is what makes density × length a good approximation. It doesn't bound \(f\).

\(X\) has pdf \(f(x) = 3x^2\) on \([0, 1]\) (and 0 elsewhere), so its cdf there is \(F(x) = x^3\). What is \(P(0.5 < X \le 0.6)\)? (A decimal to three places or an expression such as 0.6^3-0.5^3.)

\(F(0.6) - F(0.5) = 0.216 - 0.125 = 0.091\). Compare density × length at the left end, \(f(0.5) \times 0.1 = 0.075\), and at the right end, \(f(0.6) \times 0.1 = 0.108\): the exact answer sits between, because the density rises across the interval.

Part 3 · Warm-ups (about 6 minutes)

These come back from lessons 7 and 8: two conditional-probability calculations, and one question on checking a theorem's hypothesis before using it.

Two fair dice are rolled. Given that at least one die shows 6, what is the probability that both show 6? (A fraction, a decimal to three places, or an expression such as 2/22; / for division.)

"At least one 6" contains 11 of the 36 rolls (6 with the first die 6, 6 with the second, minus (6,6) counted twice); one of them is (6,6). So \(1/11 \approx 0.091\). Compare "given the first die shows 6": 6 rolls, answer \(1/6\). Different conditions, different answers.

Adapted from Casella & Berger, Example 1.3.6 and Exercise 1.41, numbers changed. Telegraph dots and dashes are sent in the proportion 5:3 (dots more common). Interference turns a dot into a dash with probability 1/5, and a dash into a dot with probability 1/5. A dash is received. What is the probability a dash was sent? (A fraction, a decimal to two places or better, or an expression; * for ×, / for division.)

\(P(\text{dash sent}) = 3/8\), \(P(\text{dot sent}) = 5/8\). \(P(\text{dash received}) = \frac45\cdot\frac38 + \frac15\cdot\frac58 = \frac{12}{40} + \frac{5}{40} = \frac{17}{40}\). So \(P(\text{dash sent} \mid \text{dash received}) = \dfrac{12/40}{17/40} = \dfrac{12}{17} \approx 0.706\). The numerator alone, \(\frac45 \cdot \frac38\), is the probability of "dash sent and dash received"; dividing by \(P(\text{dash received})\) is what makes it conditional.

Two fair dice. \(A\) = the first die shows 6, \(B\) = the sum is 12. Which step is wrong?

  1. \(P(A) = 6/36 = 1/6\) and \(P(B) = 1/36\).
  2. By Axiom 3, \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) = 7/36\).
  3. So the probability that the first die shows 6 or the sum is 12 is 7/36.

Axiom 3 adds probabilities only for disjoint events, and these aren't: (6,6) is in both (in fact \(B \subseteq A\)). Check a theorem's hypothesis before using it. Here \(A \cup B = A\), so the right answer is \(1/6 = 6/36\), not \(7/36\). The same check is why, in a proof, "the sets are pairwise disjoint" has to come before "by Axiom 3".

Day 2 starts here.

Part 4 · Identically distributed (new, about 4 minutes)

From the reading. One Chapter 1 idea we skipped, and it matters from Chapter 5 on, where a sample is "\(X_1, \dots, X_n\), identically distributed".

Two different functions. Toss a fair coin three times. \(X\) = number of heads, \(Y\) = number of tails. On the outcome HHT, \(X = 2\) and \(Y = 1\). They're different functions on \(S\); in fact \(X(s) + Y(s) = 3\) for every outcome.

Same probabilities. \(P(X = k)\) and \(P(Y = k)\) are both \(1, 3, 3, 1\) out of 8 for \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\) (swap H and T in each outcome). So for every set \(A\) of numbers, \(P(X \in A) = P(Y \in A)\).

Name it. That is Definition 1.5.8: \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed. Theorem 1.5.10 says this is the same as having the same cdf, \(F_X(x) = F_Y(x)\) for every \(x\). It does not say \(X = Y\): here they're never equal.

A fair coin is tossed four times. \(X\) = number of heads, \(Y\) = number of tails. They're identically distributed. For how many of the 16 equally likely outcomes is \(X(s) = Y(s)\)?

\(X = Y\) means two heads and two tails: \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) outcomes. So \(P(X = Y) = 6/16\), not 1: identically distributed variables can agree on some outcomes, on none (three tosses), or on all, and none of that is part of the definition.

\(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed random variables. Which statement must be true?

Theorem 1.5.10: identically distributed is equivalent to equal cdfs at every \(x\); agreeing at one point isn't enough. It never requires \(X = Y\) (three-toss heads and tails are never equal), and \(1 - F_Y\) isn't even a cdf (it falls from 1 to 0).

Part 5 · Chapter 1 on one page (about 8 minutes)

Beyond the reading: a map of the whole chapter. Each arrow points from an idea to one built on it; the dashed arrow is Theorem 1.5.10.

Now recall each one from memory. Say it out loud or write it, then flip the card and mark yourself honestly.

State Kolmogorov's three axioms, and say what they're for.

For every event \(A\): (1) \(P(A) \ge 0\); (2) \(P(S) = 1\); (3) for pairwise disjoint \(A_1, A_2, \dots\), \(P(\bigcup A_i) = \sum P(A_i)\). For: every other rule in probability is proved from these three.

State the complement rule and monotonicity, and say what each is for.

\(P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\) (Theorem 1.2.8c); if \(A \subseteq B\) then \(P(A) \le P(B)\) (Theorem 1.2.9c). For: "at least one" problems (take the complement of "none"), and bounds (a cdf is nondecreasing because of monotonicity).

Define conditional probability and state Bayes' rule, including what it assumes.

\(P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)\), for \(P(B) > 0\). Bayes: if \(A_1, A_2, \dots\) partition \(S\) and \(P(B) > 0\), \(P(A_i \mid B) = P(B \mid A_i)P(A_i) \big/ \sum_j P(B \mid A_j)P(A_j)\). For: turning "probability of the evidence given the cause" into "probability of the cause given the evidence" (the Morse code problem).

Define independence of two events, and say how mutual independence of three differs from pairwise.

\(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\): learning one doesn't change the probability of the other. Three events are mutually independent when every pair and the triple satisfy the product rule; pairwise alone isn't enough (the \(S = \{1,2,3,4\}\) counterexample). For: computing joint probabilities by multiplying, as in de Méré's dice and every "independent sample" later.

Define a random variable and the probability it induces.

A function \(X: S \to \mathbb{R}\). Induced probability: \(P_X(X \in A) = P(\{s \in S : X(s) \in A\})\). For: moving from events to numbers, which is the language of the rest of the book.

Define the cdf and state the three properties that characterize cdfs.

\(F_X(x) = P(X \le x)\) for every real \(x\). A function is a cdf exactly when (a) its limits are 0 at \(-\infty\) and 1 at \(+\infty\), (b) it is nondecreasing, (c) it is right-continuous (Theorem 1.5.3). For: one function that describes any random variable, discrete, continuous or mixed; \(P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)\).

Say what a pmf and a pdf are, and the two conditions that make a function one (Theorem 1.6.5).

Pmf: \(f(x) = P(X = x)\) (discrete). Pdf: \(F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt\) (continuous); \(f\) is a density, not a probability. Both: \(f \ge 0\), and the total (sum or integral) is 1. For: computing probabilities by summing or integrating, and checking a proposed model is a real distribution (normalizing constants).

Define "identically distributed" and say what it does not mean.

\(P(X \in A) = P(Y \in A)\) for every set \(A\), equivalently \(F_X = F_Y\) (Theorem 1.5.10). It does not mean \(X = Y\). For: the "identically distributed" half of every random sample from Chapter 5 on.

That's Chapter 1. The chapter check comes next: recall questions across all six sections and one proof.

Extra practice (optional)

From Casella & Berger, Chapter 1 exercises (easiest first; worked solutions are in the Casella & Berger solutions manual):

  1. Exercise 1.38 (a) and (b): conditional probability when \(P(B) = 1\) and when \(A \subseteq B\).
  2. Exercise 1.39: prove that events with positive probability can't be both mutually exclusive and independent.
  3. Exercise 1.40 (c): finish Theorem 1.3.9 by proving \(A^c\) and \(B^c\) are independent (part b is the proof in Part 1).
  4. Exercise 1.44: a 20-question multiple-choice test with independent guessing; at least 10 right.

Extra reading: John Haigh, Probability: A Very Short Introduction, Chapter 2 ("The workings of probability"), the section "Independence" (about 2 pages, in your library). It has a die where independence is not obvious, and asks you to redo it with eight- and ten-sided dice: one gives independent events, the other doesn't.

Extra article: Adam Molnar, "High school mathematics teachers' understanding of independent events" (ICME-13, 2016):

. Of 25 high-school math teachers asked whether two events in a table were independent, only three gave a correctly explained answer, and many were confident in wrong ones. It traces the confusion to the other meanings of "independent", including algebra's independent variable, which fixes the dependent one exactly.
